items.question: What Is a VPN?
items.answer: A VPN is a service that encrypts your internet connection and hides your real location. Encryption means turning your data into a secret code that only you and the VPN can read.

items.question: Why Does This Matter to You Personally?
items.answer: Public WiFi Protection: When you use WiFi at Starbucks, anyone nearby can intercept your data. Hackers set up fake WiFi hotspots to steal passwords. A VPN stops this instantly.

items.question: Q: Does a VPN slow down my internet?
items.answer: A: Slightly, yes. Encryption takes processing power. A quality VPN should only slow you by 10-30%. If Netflix loads in five seconds instead of four, you probably won't notice. If everything crawls, your VPN might be overloaded or far away.

items.question: Q: Can my internet provider still see what I'm doing with a VPN?
items.answer: A: No. Your ISP sees encrypted traffic going to a VPN server. They can't see what websites you visit or what you download. They only see you're using a VPN—not your actual activity.

items.question: Q: Is using a VPN illegal?
items.answer: A: In most countries, no. VPNs are legal in the US, UK, Canada, and most of Europe. A few countries restrict them. Using a VPN for illegal activities is still illegal—the VPN doesn't change that.

items.question: What's Next?
items.answer: Now you understand exactly how a VPN protects you online. You know it encrypts your data, hides your location, and keeps hackers out of your business.

items.question: What is Website Security?
items.answer: Website security is the set of protections that keep attackers out of your site and keep visitor information safe.

items.question: How Does Website Security Work?
items.answer: Good website security uses layers. If one control fails, another one still reduces the damage.

items.question: Does my website need SSL if I do not sell anything?
items.answer: Yes. SSL protects forms, logins, comments, and visitor trust. Browsers and search engines also expect HTTPS.

items.question: How much will website security cost?
items.answer: Many essentials are free: SSL from your host, Cloudflare's basic plan, password managers with free tiers, and platform security updates. The main cost is consistency.

items.question: What should I do if my website gets hacked?
items.answer: Take the site offline if sensitive data may be exposed, contact your host, restore a clean backup, scan for malware, change all passwords, patch the weakness, and notify affected users if required.

items.question: What is a Database?
items.answer: A database is a digital filing cabinet. It stores your data (customer names, video lists, chat messages) in an organized way. You ask it for information, and it retrieves it instantly.

items.question: What is SQL?
items.answer: SQL (Structured Query Language) is the organized filing cabinet. Everything has a fixed drawer, label, and place. Think: a spreadsheet with columns (name, email, phone) and rows (each person).

items.question: What is NoSQL?
items.answer: NoSQL (Not Only SQL) is the flexible filing cabinet. You throw data in however it fits. No fixed drawers. No strict labels. It adapts to what you give it.

items.question: Q1: Is SQL dying in 2026?
items.answer: No. SQL is more popular than ever. Companies in 2026 use both. SQL handles critical business data. NoSQL handles everything else. Think of it as "SQL isn't dying, it's specializing."

items.question: Q2: Can I switch from SQL to NoSQL later?
items.answer: Yes, but it's painful. Migrating data is time-consuming and risky. You'll miss your deadline and spend extra money. Choose carefully upfront.

items.question: Q3: Which is cheaper for my startup?
items.answer: SQL databases are usually cheaper. PostgreSQL and MySQL are free, open-source options. NoSQL can be pricey as your data grows.

items.question: What is an Operating System?
items.answer: An operating system is the software that manages a computer's hardware (CPU, memory, storage, network) and provides the platform on which applications run.

items.question: Can I keep using an OS after its end-of-life date?
items.answer: Technically yes — the OS keeps running — but it stops receiving security patches, making it increasingly risky over time. Extended Security Update (ESU) programs exist for some products (like Windows 10) at a cost.

items.question: What's the difference between "standard support" and "extended support"?
items.answer: Standard support includes new features plus security and bug fixes. Extended support (or LTS/ESM in the Linux world) usually only includes critical security patches, with no new features.

items.question: Why do Linux LTS releases last longer than regular releases?
items.answer: Long Term Support (LTS) releases are specifically built for production stability — vendors commit to years of patches instead of months, which is why most servers run LTS versions rather than the latest release.

items.question: What is Phishing?
items.answer: Phishing is a social-engineering attack that uses fake messages — usually email, but also text, voice calls, or chat — to trick you into giving up credentials, clicking a malicious link, or taking an action that helps the attacker.

items.question: Can opening a phishing email alone infect my device?
items.answer: Simply opening a plain-text email is very unlikely to infect you, but opening attachments, enabling macros, or clicking links inside it can. Treat any unexpected attachment or link with caution, regardless of whether you've already "opened" the email.

items.question: How can I tell a real bank email from a fake one?
items.answer: Check the actual sender address (not just the name), hover over links to confirm they point to the bank's real domain, and remember that banks generally don't ask you to "confirm your password" via an emailed link. When in doubt, log in directly through the bank's app or by typing the address yourself.

items.question: What's the difference between phishing and a data breach?
items.answer: Phishing is a method of attack (tricking a person into giving up access). A data breach is often the result — phishing is one of the most common ways attackers gain the access needed to cause a breach in the first place.

items.question: Does antivirus software stop phishing?
items.answer: Antivirus and email filters block a meaningful share of phishing attempts and malicious attachments, but well-crafted phishing messages and brand-new lookalike domains regularly slip through. Human awareness remains a necessary second layer.

items.question: What is Ransomware?
items.answer: Ransomware is software that denies you access to your own files or systems — usually by encrypting them — until you pay the attacker, with no guarantee they'll actually restore access.

items.question: Should You Pay the Ransom?
items.answer: Law enforcement agencies, including the FBI and most national cybersecurity authorities, generally advise against paying. The reasons are practical, not just ethical:

items.question: Can I remove ransomware without losing my files?
items.answer: You can remove the malware itself, but removing it doesn't decrypt files that are already encrypted. Getting files back requires either a backup, a known decryptor for that specific ransomware family, or, in rare cases, paying the ransom.

items.question: Will antivirus remove ransomware after the fact?
items.answer: Antivirus can usually detect and delete the ransomware program itself, but it generally cannot decrypt files that have already been encrypted. Removal and decryption are two separate problems.

items.question: How do I know if my backups are safe from ransomware?
items.answer: If your backup storage is reachable from the same network and credentials as your main systems, it should be treated as at risk. Offline backups, or backups with separate, isolated credentials and immutability settings, are far safer.

items.question: Is ransomware only a risk for big companies?
items.answer: No. Individuals and small businesses are common targets precisely because they often have weaker defenses and are more likely to pay smaller ransoms quickly.
